RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (CNN)  -- The Taliban in Afghanistan have momentum that makes any effort to negotiate with them difficult, the U.S. defense secretary said. Defense Secretary Robert Gates arrived in Cairo, Egypt, on Monday. He's visiting Afghanistan on Wednesday. Secretary Robert Gates spoke to CNN's Chris Lawrence in an exclusive interview Tuesday evening before leaving for Afghanistan, where he is visiting troops and bases Wednesday. "The political level of the Taliban probably isn't ready to think about reconciliation or any kind of accommodation at this point," Gates said in the interview. "They probably feel like they have the momentum with them. And until that momentum changes, it will be difficult." As part of the U.S. strategy in Afghanistan, the military and Afghanistan government are attempting to reach out to elements of the Taliban who are engaged in the battle for financial gain, rather than ideological gain. "There are really two groups we're talking about -- the younger, or less committed, who do this mainly to earn a living and put food on the table for their families, and those that are more ideologically committed. The latter are going to be a tougher pull, and we'll probably have to wait awhile before there's an opportunity there." On Monday, CNN's Nic Robertson interviewed a spokesman for the Taliban, Zabiullah Mujahid, who said the Taliban will only negotiate with the Afghanistan government when the United States leaves the country. "Our conditions are clear, we want to negotiate and they [the U.S.] will not interfere in our affairs; secondly, they [the U.S.] will leave the country," Mujahid told CNN. Gates said the stance was not surprising. "Well I don't know what else he'd say. He's leading the opposition, he's leading this insurgency. He's not going to sort of, sort of throw down and say 'We're ready to negotiate, we're about done here,' " Gates said. The United States is adding 21,000 troops to the Afghanistan battlefield. The majority will be moving to the south to confront the Taliban along the porous Pakistani border. The Taliban have had mostly free rein in that area with few U.S. or coalition forces to confront them until now. Gates admitted moving the battle to the south will mean there is "a tough fight ahead." "I think, certainly, I have been pretty clear. As we move into areas of the south that have not seen any Afghan or coalition forces so far, we're clearly going to be going into areas where the Taliban are very entrenched," he said. "And, sad to say, I expect with the rising level of our activity and operations, there probably will be higher casualties." In recent weeks, the Pakistani government has seen the Taliban gain control on its side of the Afghanistan-Pakistan border. Privately, Pakistani officials have expressed concern to the United States that the increased fighting in southern Afghanistan will only push the Taliban back to the Pakistani side. "Well I think it's just the reality that there are extremists on both sides of that border. And they threaten both the elected government of Afghanistan and the elected government of Pakistan. So like it or not, they both have a certain common enemy," Gates said. Gates said he is encouraged by recent cooperation efforts between the two countries to deal with the problem, and by Pakistan's recent confrontation with the Taliban in Bunir province, near the capital of Islamabad. "The signs right now are pretty positive," he told CNN.

***

**RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (CNN)** — The Taliban’s current battlefield momentum in Afghanistan severely complicates any immediate prospects for peace negotiations, U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates stated. 

Following a visit to Cairo on Monday, Gates spoke exclusively with CNN’s Chris Lawrence on Tuesday evening prior to traveling to Afghanistan, where he is scheduled to inspect troops and military bases on Wednesday.

"The political leadership of the Taliban is likely unprepared to entertain reconciliation or any form of accommodation at this juncture," Gates noted. "They perceive that momentum is on their side, and until that dynamic shifts, diplomatic progress will remain elusive."

As part of the broader U.S. strategy, American and Afghan forces are attempting to engage pragmatic, financially motivated Taliban fighters rather than ideological hardliners. 

"There are essentially two distinct groups we are talking about," Gates explained. "The younger, less committed fighters who participate primarily to earn a living and feed their families, and those who are deeply committed ideologically. The latter will be a much tougher pull, and it will take time before a viable opportunity emerges."

Earlier on Monday, Taliban spokesman Zabiullah Mujahid told CNN’s Nic Robertson that the insurgent group would engage with the Afghan government only after a complete U.S. troop withdrawal and an end to foreign interference. 

Gates dismissed the spokesman's statement as predictable posturing. "I don't know what else he would say," Gates remarked. "He is leading an active insurgency; he is hardly going to stand down and announce that they are ready to negotiate or finished fighting."

To alter the battlefield dynamics, the United States is deploying an additional 21,000 troops. The majority will be stationed in the south to secure the porous border with Pakistan—a region where the Taliban have operated with relative impunity due to a historically sparse U.S. and coalition presence.

Gates acknowledged that pushing into these strongholds portends a grueling campaign ahead. 

"As we advance into areas of the south that have not previously seen Afghan or coalition forces, we are entering territories where the Taliban are deeply entrenched," Gates cautioned. "Regrettably, as the scale of our operations escalates, we must anticipate higher casualties."

Meanwhile, amid expanding Taliban influence along its side of the border, Pakistani officials have privately expressed concern to Washington that an intensified U.S. offensive in southern Afghanistan could drive militants back into Pakistan.

Gates addressed these concerns by emphasizing the mutual nature of the threat: "The reality is that extremists inhabit both sides of that border, threatening the democratically elected governments of both Afghanistan and Pakistan. Like it or not, both nations share a common enemy."

Despite these challenges, Gates expressed optimism regarding recent cross-border security cooperation, highlighting Pakistan’s recent military offensive against the Taliban in Buner province near the capital of Islamabad. 

"The current signs are quite positive," Gates concluded.

**Headline:** Shifting the Battlefield Dynamic: The Dual Strategy of Escalation and Reconciliation in Afghanistan

As the security situation in Afghanistan continues to deteriorate, the United States is recalibrating its strategy to confront a resurgence of Taliban momentum. Facing a formidable insurgency that has expanded its reach across key provinces, Washington is pursuing a high-stakes, dual-track approach: combining a significant military escalation with targeted political overtures. By deploying 21,000 additional U.S. troops while simultaneously attempting to splinter the insurgency from within, the administration hopes to alter the balance of power on the ground and ultimately force a path toward stability.

### The Military Surge: Reclaiming the Initiative

The centerpiece of the immediate U.S. response is a reinforcement of 21,000 military personnel, comprising combat brigades, support units, and military trainers. This infusion of forces aims to secure vulnerable population centers, disrupt Taliban safe havens, and provide critical support to the expanding Afghan National Security Forces. 

For months, commanders on the ground have warned that the Taliban’s growing operational strength has undermined public confidence in the Afghan central government. By deploying additional boots on the ground, the military objective is clear: halt the momentum of the insurgency, reverse their territorial gains, and establish a security envelope that allows local governance and development to take root.

### Fracturing the Insurgency: Ideology vs. Opportunism

Alongside the military surge, American policy is adopting a more nuanced view of the enemy. Recognizing that the insurgency is not a monolithic bloc, U.S. strategists are seeking to differentiate between hardline, radicalized Taliban commanders and the broader rank-and-file fighters. 

A substantial portion of the insurgency is comprised of "ten-dollar Taliban"—local men driven to take up arms not by radical Islamist theology, but by economic necessity, tribal grievances, or a lack of alternative livelihoods. To capitalize on this vulnerability, the U.S. and its international allies are backing economic initiatives, community engagement efforts, and reintegration programs designed to peel these less ideologically committed fighters away from the battlefield. By offering financial alternatives, security guarantees, and a path back into their communities, the strategy seeks to deplete the Taliban’s manpower from the bottom up.

### The Gates Assessment: No Peace Without Leverage

However, attempts to engage the core Taliban leadership have hit a formidable wall. U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates offered a stark assessment of the prospects for high-level political talks, stating unequivocally that the top leadership of the Taliban currently has no interest in reconciling with the Afghan government or international coalition.

Speaking on the strategic reality of the conflict, Secretary Gates emphasized that as long as the Taliban believe they are winning, they have no incentive to compromise. Powerful insurgent leaders, operating comfortably from sanctuary zones, view the current trajectory as leaning in their favor. Under these conditions, any offer of peace negotiations is perceived by the Taliban not as an opportunity for compromise, but as a sign of Western weakness and fatigue.

### Battlefield Realities as a Prerequisite for Peace

The Secretary’s analysis underscores a fundamental principle of counterinsurgency and diplomatic strategy: political resolutions are rarely achieved without military leverage. For meaningful negotiations to occur, the Taliban’s leadership must be convinced that military victory is impossible.

Consequently, the U.S. strategy hinges on the belief that altering the battlefield dynamic is an indispensable prerequisite for any future political settlement. The 21,000 additional troops are not intended to achieve a purely military victory—which policy experts widely agree is unattainable in Afghanistan—but rather to create the necessary conditions for a political solution. 

By applying intense military pressure on hardliners while offering an off-ramp to pragmatists and economic insurgents, the U.S. hopes to push the Taliban toward a tipping point. Only when the insurgent leadership faces unsustainable losses and diminishing manpower will the prospect of a genuine, negotiated peace transition from a distant hope to a realistic outcome.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a news article about Defense Secretary Robert Gates discussing U.S. strategy in Afghanistan and the likelihood of negotiating with the Taliban.
counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON** — Defense Secretary Robert M. Gates acknowledged that the United States will ultimately need to engage in negotiations with elements of the Taliban to end the conflict in Afghanistan, though he emphasized that serious peace talks cannot happen until coalition forces reverse the insurgents' momentum on the battlefield.

Speaking during a series of interviews detailing the administration's broader strategy for the region, Gates offered a pragmatic assessment of the nearly decade-long war, noting that most insurgencies throughout history have ended with a political settlement rather than a total military victory.

“You don’t make peace with your friends, you make peace with your enemies,” Gates said. “Ultimately, there has to be a political resolution to this conflict. But the timing is critical.”

According to Gates, the success of any future reconciliation depends directly on the current military strategy, which includes the deployment of tens of thousands of additional U.S. troops to key strongholds in southern Afghanistan, such as Helmand and Kandahar provinces. Gates argued that until the Taliban feels sufficient military pressure and begins losing ground, its leaders will have little incentive to come to the negotiating table in good faith.

“The key is to change the momentum on the ground so that the Taliban leadership recognizes that they cannot win,” Gates explained. “Only when they realize that time is not on their side will you see genuine interest in reconciliation.”

The Defense Secretary outlined strict, non-negotiable conditions for any Taliban fighters or factions seeking to re-enter Afghan political life. Any reconciled insurgents, he said, must lay down their arms, sever all ties with Al Qaeda, and agree to abide by the Afghan constitution, including its protections for the rights of women and minorities.

Gates also drew a sharp distinction between hardline ideological leaders—such as Mullah Mohammad Omar—and lower-level fighters who have joined the insurgency for money or due to local tribal grievances. 

“There are hardliners who will never reconcile, and they will have to be eliminated or captured,” Gates said. “But there are also many rank-and-file fighters who are essentially mercenaries or acting out of local discontent. A major part of our strategy is to split those individuals away from the core leadership.”

The Secretary's comments reflect a growing consensus within the Obama administration and NATO leadership that military operations are meant to create space for a broader political outcome. Afghan President Hamid Karzai has increasingly pushed for dialogue with the Taliban, establishing a High Peace Council to explore potential avenues for talks.

However, Gates’ remarks also reflect lingering caution within the U.S. national security establishment. Skeptics on Capitol Hill and within the intelligence community have warned that the Taliban may use the prospect of negotiations as a delay tactic, waiting out the timetable for U.S. troop withdrawals.

Despite these concerns, Gates reiterated that military force alone cannot resolve the underlying political and social drivers of the war.

“Military operations are essential to creating the right conditions,” Gates said. “But at the end of the day, the future of Afghanistan will be decided by Afghans sitting down with Afghans to determine how they are going to govern their country.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Pretend you are a CNN journalist in May 2009 reporting from Riyadh. Write a news dispatch detailing Defense Secretary Robert Gates' interview with Chris Lawrence about Taliban momentum, U.S. troop increases, and border dynamics with Pakistan.
counterfactuals.output:
**RIYADH, Saudi Arabia (CNN)** — Defense Secretary Robert Gates offered a candid and sober assessment of the war in Afghanistan today, acknowledging that the Taliban currently holds the momentum on the ground, but expressing firm confidence that an incoming wave of U.S. troops will turn the tide.

Speaking with CNN Pentagon Correspondent Chris Lawrence during a diplomatic stop in the Saudi capital, Gates addressed the escalating violence along the Afghan-Pakistan border, the expanding U.S. military footprint in South Asia, and the growing political political will in Islamabad to confront militant networks.

"The Taliban have momentum right now," Gates told Lawrence. "And our goal over the next 12 to 18 months, with the additional troops President Obama has authorized, is to reverse that momentum—to take away their initiative and secure the population."

### A Critical Surge in Southern Afghanistan

Gates’ stop in Riyadh comes amid a whirlwind tour of the region as the Obama administration rolls out its revamped "Af-Pak" strategy. President Obama has ordered roughly 21,000 additional U.S. forces to Afghanistan—primarily Marines and Army combat units destined for the Taliban's heartland in the south and east.

In his conversation with Lawrence, Gates emphasized that the extra boots on the ground are essential to changing the dynamic before public and political support in the West wears thin. However, the Defense Secretary reiterated his longstanding caution against creating an oversized American military footprint that could alienate the local population.

"We have to demonstrate progress," Gates said, acknowledging the growing war weariness after nearly eight years of conflict. "We have to show that the Afghan government, with our assistance and the assistance of our coalition partners, can provide security and basic governance."

### Eyeball to Eyeball at the Pakistan Border

A major focus of the interview was the volatile, porous border separating Afghanistan from Pakistan’s Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA). For years, U.S. officials have expressed frustration over the safe havens enjoyed by the Taliban and Al Qaeda inside Pakistan.

However, Gates pointed to recent military operations launched by the Pakistani army in the Swat Valley as a sign of a significant shift in Islamabad's posture. As Pakistani forces battle militants just 60 miles from the capital, Gates told Lawrence he believes the Pakistani leadership and public now recognize the Taliban as an existential threat to their own nation.

"I think there has been a real awakening in Pakistan over the last several weeks," Gates observed. "The Pakistani military and the government now see that the internal threat posed by extremists is just as dangerous, if not more dangerous, than any traditional external threat."

Gates noted that as Pakistani forces pressure militants on their side of the border, the additional U.S. forces arriving in Afghanistan will create a "hammer and anvil" effect, preventing insurgents from slipping back and forth across the border to escape pressure.

### High-Stakes Diplomacy in Riyadh

While South Asia remains the central focus of the military strategy, Gates’ presence in Riyadh highlights the diplomatic effort to rally regional allies behind the U.S. mission. Saudi Arabia, a key Sunni power, plays a critical role in regional stability and holds potential leverage in coaxing moderate elements of the Taliban toward reconciliation—a concept Gates has previously suggested might eventually be necessary to achieve long-term peace.

During his meetings with Saudi King Abdullah and senior defense officials, Gates sought to reassure Gulf partners of the U.S. commitment to regional security, addressing not only the conflict in Afghanistan and Pakistan, but also shared concerns regarding Iran’s nuclear ambitions.

For now, however, the Secretary's message from Riyadh is clear: the road ahead in Afghanistan will be difficult, the fighting this summer will be fierce, but the administration believes it finally has the right strategy and resources to regain control of the conflict.

*Reporting from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia for CNN.*

**GATES WARNS OF RISING CASUALTIES IN AFGHAN SURGE, SAYS TALIBAN NOT READY FOR PEACE TALKS**

**BYLINE:** Staff Correspondent  
**DATELINE:** KABUL, Afghanistan  

U.S. Defense Secretary Robert M. Gates concluded a high-stakes, multi-nation tour of the Middle East and Afghanistan today, delivering a stark assessment of the conflict: American and NATO forces must prepare for an inevitable rise in casualties as a massive troop surge gets underway, and expectations for near-term peace negotiations with the Taliban are premature.

Speaking to troops and reporters in Kabul following consultations with Afghan President Hamid Karzai and key commanders on the ground, Gates laid out the strategic logic behind the Obama administration's deployment of 30,000 additional U.S. troops. 

Gates made clear that while political resolution remains the ultimate goal of the war, military momentum must shift dramatically before meaningful talks can occur.

### "They Believe They Are Winning"

Addressing widespread speculation regarding potential peace talks between the Afghan government and insurgent leaders, Gates poured cold water on the prospect of immediate political reconciliation. 

"The Taliban must be convinced that they cannot win before they will be ready for serious political reconciliation," Gates said during a joint press conference in Kabul. "Right now, the Taliban leadership believes they have the upper hand. They have no incentive to negotiate in good faith when they think time is on their side. Only sustained military pressure will change their calculus."

Gates emphasized that reconciliation cannot happen from a position of weakness. Until NATO and Afghan forces clear the insurgents from key strongholds in southern provinces like Helmand and Kandahar, the hardline Taliban leadership will remain uninterested in laying down their arms or accepting the Afghan constitution.

### Ideological vs. Economic Fighters

While expressing skepticism about high-level talks with top insurgent leaders, Gates drew a sharp distinction between the core leadership of the movement and the rank-and-file insurgents fighting on the ground—a distinction central to the U.S. military’s reintegration strategy.

"There is a fundamental difference between the ideological fighters and the economic fighters," Gates explained. 

"The ideological hardliners—those deeply aligned with Al-Qaeda and committed to the extremist vision of Mullah Omar—are unlikely to ever reconcile," he said. "They must be captured or killed. But a large portion of the insurgency consists of economic fighters: local men who take up arms simply because they are paid a few dollars a day, because of local grievances, or because they feel they have no other choice to protect their families."

Gates argued that by securing population centers and offering viable economic alternatives, the coalition can peel away these "ten-dollar-a-day" fighters, draining the Taliban of its manpower even as its core leadership refuses to negotiate.

### A Warning on Rising Casualties

The Secretary’s visit comes at a crucial juncture as thousands of additional U.S. Marines and Army infantry units stream into Afghanistan. Gates delivered an unvarnished warning to the American public and military families: the push into previously unchallenged Taliban territories will come at a heavy cost.

"As more troops go in and we take the offensive into areas that have been under Taliban control for several years, we can fully expect higher casualties," Gates warned. "The fighting will be tough. It will be bloody. But taking these strongholds back is essential to establishing security for the Afghan people and allowing the government to extend its reach."

Military commanders expect the spring and summer fighting seasons to be among the violent of the multi-year war, as U.S.-led forces contest insurgent safe havens in the south and east.

### Broad Regional Strategy

Gates’ stop in Afghanistan followed high-level diplomatic meetings across the Middle East, including stops in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Throughout his regional tour, the Defense Secretary sought to shore up support for the Afghanistan strategy while addressing shared security concerns regarding Iran’s nuclear ambitions.

In conversations with Gulf allies, Gates urged partner nations to assist in choking off private financial flows from wealthy donors in the region to the Taliban—funding that directly sustains the insurgency's economic fighters.

As he departed Kabul, Gates expressed cautious confidence in the military plan crafted by General Stanley McChrystal, the top U.S. commander in Afghanistan, while reinforcing that the road ahead would be grueling.

"We have the right strategy, the right commander, and soon, the right level of resources," Gates said. "But success will require patience, grit, and a realistic understanding of the sacrifices that lie ahead."

Here is a news article written in the style and context of CNN’s coverage from **March 2009**, following President Barack Obama’s announcement of a new strategy for Afghanistan and Pakistan, and Defense Secretary Robert Gates’ subsequent media appearances.

***

**CNN.com** / POLITICS

# Gates: 21,000 troop surge key to eventual Taliban talks, Pakistan border security

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Defense Secretary Robert Gates said Sunday that the deployment of 21,000 additional U.S. troops to Afghanistan is essential to reversing the Taliban’s momentum, a necessary first step if the U.S. hopes to eventually broker political negotiations and force Pakistan to secure its border.

Speaking in an exclusive interview on CNN’s *State of the Union*, Gates outlined the Obama administration’s newly unveiled "Af-Pak" strategy, emphasizing that military power alone will not end the nearly eight-year-old war. However, he insisted that the security situation must improve before any diplomatic breakthroughs can occur.

"You don't negotiate from a position of weakness," Gates told CNN's John King. "Right now, the Taliban think they are winning. Until we can change that momentum and convince their rank-and-file fighters that they cannot prevail, political reconciliation is simply not going to happen."

### A Strategy Shift: 21,000 Troops

The Defense Secretary’s comments follow President Barack Obama’s decision to send 17,000 combat troops and 4,000 military trainers to Afghanistan ahead of the country’s planned presidential elections in August. 

The 21,000-troop surge brings the total U.S. footprint in Afghanistan to roughly 68,000 forces by the end of the summer, reflecting a dramatic pivot in focus from Iraq to Central Asia.

Gates acknowledged that the American public is grow weary of the conflict, which began in late 2001, but argued that the additional troops are vital to securing vulnerable populations, particularly in southern Afghanistan where the Taliban remains entrenched.

"The goal here is not to transform Afghanistan into a Western-style democracy," Gates said. "The goal is to prevent al Qaeda from returning, and to ensure that the Afghan government can secure its own country. To do that, we need to build up the Afghan National Army and Police, which is what these 4,000 trainers are designed to do."

### Splitting the Taliban

A central pillar of the new strategy involves separating low-level Taliban fighters from the movement’s hardcore leadership. Gates suggested that many insurgents are "local foot soldiers" driven by economic necessity or tribal grievances rather than radical Islamist ideology.

"There are individuals who fight for the Taliban simply because they are paid $10 a day, or because they are angry at local government corruption," Gates said. "Those are the people who can be reintegrated into Afghan society if we offer them an alternative."

However, Gates drew a hard line regarding senior Taliban leaders, such as Mullah Omar, who remain aligned with al Qaeda. "The hardcore extremists who refuse to renounce violence and break ties with al Qaeda must be eliminated or captured," he warned.

### Pressure on the Pakistan Border

Gates also addressed the critical issue of Pakistan's porous border, specifically the Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA), which have long served as a safe haven for Taliban militants and al Qaeda leadership launching attacks into eastern Afghanistan.

The Secretary noted a growing recognition within Islamabad that the insurgent threat poses an existential danger to Pakistan itself.

"The border region is a common threat to both Afghanistan and Pakistan," Gates said. "We are seeing better cooperation from the Pakistani military than we did a year ago, but much more needs to be done to secure that border and disrupt those safe havens."

While Gates declined to comment directly on ongoing U.S. drone strikes targeting militant leaders inside Pakistan, he stressed that the U.S. will continue to use all necessary tools to protect American forces operating along the border.

### Managing Expectations

Despite the influx of troops and resources, Gates urged patience, warning that the surge in forces would likely lead to an increase in U.S. casualties in the coming months as coalition forces push deeper into Taliban-controlled territory.

"It is going to be a tough fight this summer," Gates admitted. "Success will not come overnight, but with this new strategy, a clear focus, and the right resources, we believe we can stabilize the situation and pave the way for a political resolution."

*** 

*CNN’s National Security Producer Chris Lawrence contributed to this report.*

**Gates: Political settlement needed in Afghanistan, but Taliban must be weakened first**

By **CNN Staff**  
Updated 4:12 PM EDT, Sunday, June 5, 2011

**(CNN) —** U.S. Secretary of Defense Robert Gates said Sunday that the war in Afghanistan will ultimately end through a political settlement with the Taliban, but stressed that coalition forces must first weaken the insurgency to force them to negotiate in good faith. 

Speaking to reporters following a series of high-level security briefings in Kabul, Gates outlined the Obama administration's dual-track strategy: applying maximum military pressure through the ongoing troop surge while laying the groundwork for eventual diplomatic reconciliation.

"Broadly speaking, military operations are designed to change the calculus of the Taliban leadership," Gates said. "You have to inflict enough damage on them, reverse their momentum, and demonstrate that they cannot win militarily before they will be serious about sitting down to talk."

Gates acknowledged that reintegrating low-level fighters and reconciling with senior Taliban commanders are essential steps toward long-term stability in the region. However, he reaffirmed the U.S. government’s non-negotiable preconditions for any formal peace process.

"The outcome of any reconciliation process must be clear," Gates said. "The Taliban must break ties with Al Qaeda, lay down their weapons, and abide by the Afghan constitution, including its protections for women and minorities. There will be no shortcuts on these fundamentals."

The Defense Secretary’s comments come as the U.S. prepares to begin a modest drawdown of the 33,000 surge troops deployed by President Barack Obama in late 2009, with the goal of transitioning primary security responsibility to Afghan forces by the end of 2014.

### Taliban Rejects U.S. Conditions

Responding to Gates’ remarks, Taliban spokesman Zabiullah Mujahid dismissed the U.S. strategy as a "delusion" and reiterated the insurgent group's long-standing refusal to enter talks while foreign troops remain in Afghanistan.

In a phone interview with CNN, Mujahid said the coalition’s military pressure had failed to break the Taliban’s resolve and characterized the U.S. focus on reconciliation as a sign of weakness.

"Robert Gates and the Americans are dreaming if they think they can force the Islamic Emirate to accept their terms through military aggression," Mujahid said. "The surge has achieved nothing except increasing casualties on both sides. They talk about peace, but they are expanding their military footprint."

Mujahid reiterated that the complete and unconditional withdrawal of all NATO-led international forces remains a prerequisite for any formal peace negotiations.

"As long as foreign invaders occupy our land and bomb our villages, talk of peace is nothing more than propaganda," Mujahid added. "Once the foreign troops leave, the Afghans can resolve their internal issues among themselves."

### A Fragile Diplomatic Horizon

Gates’ comments reflect a growing consensus within Washington and international capitals that the decade-long conflict cannot be resolved solely on the battlefield. Afghan President Hamid Karzai has stepped up efforts through the newly formed High Peace Council to open indirect channels with insurgent representatives, though tangible progress has remained elusive.

U.S. defense officials privately acknowledge that preliminary exploratory contacts have occurred, but caution that formal peace talks remain distant. 

As he prepares to step down as Defense Secretary at the end of the month, Gates stressed that patience and sustained commitment are required to secure a lasting peace.

"Reconciliation is not something that happens overnight, and it rarely happens when one side feels it is winning," Gates said. "Our task right now is to ensure the Taliban understand that their path forward lies through politics, not the battlefield."
